title: Inference for the Difference in Two Proportions

steps.instruction: The Malaria Vaccine dataset randomly assigned children to vaccine or control and recorded who got infected. The question: does the vaccine CHANGE the infection rate? State H₀ and Hₐ in your head.
steps.observe: Is this naturally one-sided or two-sided?
steps.reveal: H₀: p₁ - p₂ = 0 vs. Hₐ: p₁ - p₂ ≠ 0. 'Change' gives no direction, so it is two-sided.

steps.instruction: Look at the per-group counts the tool reports. Compute (or read) the pooled proportion \(\hat{p}\) and check n<sub>i</sub> · \(\hat{p}\) and n<sub>i</sub> · (1 - \(\hat{p}\)) for both groups.
steps.observe: Are all four counts at least 10?
steps.reveal: For the malaria data both groups have plenty of successes and failures - success-failure condition is met. Normal approximation is fine here.

steps.instruction: Run the two-sided z-test. Read off z, the p-value, and the 95% CI for p₁ - p₂.
steps.observe: Does the CI contain 0? Does the p-value reject H₀ at α = 0.05?
steps.reveal: CI and test always agree: the test rejects H₀ at α = 0.05 exactly when the 95% CI excludes 0. For the malaria data the CI typically lies entirely below 0 - lower infection rate in the vaccine group.

steps.instruction: Write a one-sentence conclusion in context. Then evaluate: 'There is a 95% probability that p₁ - p₂ lies in this interval.'
steps.reveal: p₁ - p₂ is a FIXED but unknown number. The 95% refers to the long-run success rate of the interval-building procedure: across many studies, 95% of intervals built this way would capture the true difference.

steps.instruction: Open /simulate/randomization-diff-props/?dataset=malaria in a new tab and run 5000 shuffles. Compare its p-value to the z-test's.
steps.reveal: On well-behaved data the randomization and z-test give nearly identical p-values. When conditions fail the simulation stays honest and the z drifts - this calibration check is what keeps the analytic answer trustworthy.
